analysis.one_liner: Requires phone and video-call charges in prisons and jails to be just and reasonable under FCC oversight.
analysis.headline: Passed the Senate unanimously and the House by voice vote, and became law in January 2023, restoring the FCC's authority to cap prison phone and video-call rates.
analysis.plain_summary: This law tells the Federal Communications Commission to make sure that charges for phone calls, and for the first time video and other electronic messages, placed by people in prisons and jails are just and reasonable. It removes a legal limit that had stopped the FCC from regulating the total cost of a call, and it orders the agency to write new rules within about two years. The point is to bring down some of the highest phone rates in the country, which are paid not by inmates but by their families on the outside.
analysis.who_benefits: The families of the roughly two million people held in U.S. prisons and jails. They pay for the calls, and for years they have paid some of the highest per-minute rates in American telecommunications — often more than $1 a minute for collect calls — plus steep fees for video visits. The law also helps inmates stay connected to family, which research links to lower re-offending.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FCC to ensure that rates and charges for prison and jail calling services, including advanced audio and video services, are just and reasonable [S2][S6].
Deletes the 'per call' language in the Communications Act that courts had used to block the FCC from capping the full cost of a call, restoring the agency's ability to regulate total rates [S7].
Extends FCC rate authority for the first time to video calls and other advanced communications services inmates use to reach people outside the facility [S7].
Orders the FCC to write implementing rules within 18 to 24 months of enactment, so the mandate has a deadline rather than sitting as an unenforced principle [S7].

analysis.who_pays: Prison telecom companies — the contractors that hold exclusive calling contracts with jails and prisons, such as Securus Technologies and Global Tel*Link — lose the excess per-minute charges and fees that made inmate calling a billion-dollar-a-year business. Inmates' families continue to pay for calls; the law regulates rates but does not make them free. The FCC must also weigh the cost of security measures when setting rates, which gives providers an argument for keeping rates higher than pure connection costs would justify.

drawbacks.text: The FCC must consider the costs of safety and security measures and differences between small, medium, and large facilities, which providers can use to argue for higher rates than the underlying call costs [S7].
Families keep paying until the FCC finishes its rulemaking, which the law allows to start as late as 24 months after enactment, and the law does not mandate free calls [S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A narrow but well-aimed law: it fixes a specific court-created obstacle and covers video calls, the fastest-growing charge on families. The main weakness is the security-cost consideration built in for providers, and the fact that relief waits on FCC rules rather than arriving with the law itself. On balance the public gain — affordable family contact for millions of households — clearly outweighs the revenue lost by the contractors.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate by unanimous consent on December 21, 2022, passed the House by voice vote the next day under a fast-track procedure, and the President signed it on January 5, 2023, making it Public Law 117-338 [S4][S5][S6][S9].

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Duckworth on May 10, 2021 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat for about ten months [S9].
The Commerce Committee, chaired by Senator Cantwell, ordered it reported favorably with a substitute amendment in March 2022 and formally reported it on December 15, 2022 [S9].
The Senate passed it by unanimous consent on December 21, 2022, during the post-election session [S4][S9].
The House passed it by voice vote on December 22, 2022 under suspension of the rules, a procedure used for bills expected to pass without opposition [S5][S9].
The President signed it on January 5, 2023, and it became Public Law 117-338 [S6][S7][S9].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Families of incarcerated people gained a path to affordable calls and video visits. Prison telecom contractors, who had charged among the highest per-minute rates in the country, are the ones who give up revenue as the FCC writes its rate rules.

for.name: Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in May 2021 and carried it through the Senate.

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee with a substitute amendment in December 2022 and placed it on the calendar for floor action.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the Senate bill, bringing it to a House vote the day after it cleared the Senate.

for.name: 13 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Cross-party cosponsor bloc (11 of 48 Senate Democrats, 1 of 50 Senate Republicans, 1 of 2 Senate independents)

for.name: President Biden
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on January 5, 2023.

against.name: Prison telecom providers (e.g., Securus Technologies, Global Tel*Link)
against.role: Contractors holding exclusive calling contracts with prisons and jails
against.what_they_did: No group opposed the bill on the record; providers had previously litigated against FCC rate caps and are widely reported to have defended their rates, but the bill itself passed with no recorded opposition.

sides.party_line_note: There was no opposition vote to divide on: the Senate passed it by unanimous consent and the House by voice vote, and its 13 Senate cosponsors included one Republican and one independent alongside eleven Democrats.

industries.industry: Prison telecom providers (jail and prison calling contractors)
industries.note: These contractors hold exclusive calling contracts with facilities and have charged families among the highest per-minute rates in U.S. telecom. The bill deletes the 'per call' limitation courts used to block FCC caps and lets the agency set just and reasonable rates, including for video calls, directly cutting their fee revenue.

industries.industry: Video visitation and tablet communications vendors
industries.note: The bill extends FCC rate authority to advanced audio and video communications for the first time, ending an unregulated channel where vendors have charged families per video visit. Vendors can still argue security costs justify rates, since the FCC must consider them.
